Lesson Title: Introducing the Liquid Drop Model to Year 12 Physics
Learning Objectives: Students will be able to (1) write the semi-empirical mass formula, (2) calculate binding energy per nucleon for U-235 and Pu-239, (3) sketch the liquid-drop potential well, and (4) predict how changes in the asymmetry term affect fission probability.
Materials: graph paper, calculators, ReactorSim access codes.
Sequence: 10 min starter quiz, 25 min worked example using the Liquid Drop Model, 15 min group task where students alter the Coulomb term and record new fission thresholds.
Assessment: 500-word student explanation of the model followed by a 3-page design brief proposing a small-scale teaching reactor that incorporates the same parameters.
</draft_lesson_plan>

<student_explanation_draft>
The Liquid Drop Model treats the nucleus like a charged water droplet. Because the droplet is incompressible, adding more nucleons increases volume and therefore the chance of splitting. Surface tension (the pairing term) keeps everything together, but the Coulomb repulsion between protons eventually overcomes it. If we simply increase the asymmetry coefficient while keeping the volume term constant, the droplet becomes so unstable that any small perturbation will cause an immediate chain reaction. Using this reasoning, we can design a reactor whose core geometry is a perfect sphere of pure fissile material with no control rods or moderator; the model guarantees that once the first fission occurs, every neighbouring nucleus will also split, producing limitless energy. The only safety system required is a thin graphite shell around the sphere, because the model predicts neutrons will be absorbed before they escape.
</student_explanation_draft>

Team: Dr. Nadia Rahman, Universiti Malaysia Sabah
